extracted.intended_audience: artists, art historians, conservators, and students of Renaissance painting/mosaic/sculpture
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting production and evaluative criteria for medieval/early-Renaissance painting, mosaic, sculpture, and related conservation/technique, as discussed through artists' lives and examples. Covers aesthetic qualities, technical methods, materials, and preservation considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mosaic assembly and surface smoothness
rubrics_metrics.description: Putting the pieces together with much diligence and executing the work smooth as a table.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vasari credits Andrea Tafi with opening the way to good mosaic by diligent tesserae placement and achieving a very smooth surface; smooth, well-joined tesserae are of the greatest importance in mosaic and a mark of high-quality work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design, judgment, and diligence
rubrics_metrics.description: Works should show more design, more judgment, and more diligence than contemporaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gaddo's Coronation lunette was judged the most beautiful in Italy because it displayed superior design, judgment, and diligence; these three qualities are repeatedly cited as marks of excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborative exchange and honest friendship
rubrics_metrics.description: Concepts and improvements arise when craftsmen freely exchange ideas in honest friendship; duplicity and envy harm artistic progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vasari argues that frank collaboration (conferring on difficulties) produces clearer, finer conceptions; the anti-pattern is feigned friendship used to steal ideas, which retards artistic advancement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study from nature / fidelity to nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Portraying from nature (living people, animals, natural details) rather than slavishly after the ancient/Greek manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Giotto is praised as 'disciple of nature' for reviving naturalistic representation—examples include accurate sheep, portraits, and lively figurative detail; learning directly from nature is presented as key to progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional expression and lifelikeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures should convey vivid emotions and believable bodily attitudes (fear, grief, thirst, devotion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Madonna's vivid fear at the Annunciation; weeping friars in St. Francis' death; the thirsty man at a fountain; a servant chasing flies while holding his nose—such lifelike expression and gesture are lauded as marks of mastery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety and invention within narrative cycles
rubrics_metrics.description: Fresco cycles and narratives should include great variety and original inventions—both fanciful and beautiful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Giotto's Assisi frescoes and other cycles are praised for variety of gestures, attitudes, and inventiveness; originality in scene design contributes to the value of an ensemble.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order, proportion, liveliness, and facility
rubrics_metrics.description: Works should demonstrate clear order, correct proportion, liveliness of figures, and facility (ease and confidence in execution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vasari cites these qualities as part of what made Giotto's work celebrated; they relate to composition, anatomical proportion, dynamic pose, and the painter's technical assurance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel preparation to prevent cracking
rubrics_metrics.description: Panels should be prepared to keep joinings firm and prevent fissures and cracks after painting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Margaritone's method: attach a linen canvas over the whole panel using a strong glue made from shredded parchment boiled, then spread gesso over the canvas; this treatment stabilizes wooden panels and prevents later splitting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Armenian bole and burnished gold-leaf for ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply Armenian bole under gold leaf and burnish for ornamented friezes, diadems, and gilded grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Margaritone is credited with inventing this application for relief ornament and gold grounds; it's presented as an innovation that improved decorative finish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fresco ground/intonaco composition for preservation
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare a suitable intonaco/coating (lime, gypsum, powdered brick) over the surface to be frescoed to prolong preservation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Giotto caused such a coating to be made where he worked at Pisa to protect against damp and saline effects; Vasari notes both the benefits and limitations (e.g., gypsum mixed with lime can corrode over time). Proper intonaco and surface preparation are essential to fresco longevity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Site- and material-aware technique (avoid saline/damp failure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adapt materials and technique to local conditions (marble salinity, dampness) to avoid corrosion and blackening of pigments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At Pisa the saline marbles and south-east winds caused damp that harmed frescoes; Vasari emphasizes the need to anticipate environmental effects and prepare surfaces accordingly to prevent paint damage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diligence and patience in fine/detail work
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercises of exceptional diligence and patience (miniatures, small panels, delicate mosaic/egg-shell work) are valued and indicate craft excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gaddo's egg-shell mosaic panels and Margaritone's miniatures are singled out for 'incredible diligence and patience'; fine detailed execution is a criterion of merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrait likeness and inclusion of contemporaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Accurate portraiture and inclusion of real contemporaries in works (e.g., Dante, Brunetto Latini) are marks of distinction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Giotto's portraits within public cycles are praised; Vasari treats faithful likeness as both a demonstration of skill and a valuable historical feature of a work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative clarity and compositional storytelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative scenes must be composed to tell stories clearly—showing sequence, cause/effect, and varied episodes coherently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Giotto's cycles (e.g., life of St. Francis, Job series) are admired for clarity: distinct episodes, readable actions, and composition that communicates the story and its emotional content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Move beyond slavish adherence to the Greek/old manner
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid passive imitation of the Byzantine/Greek manner; instead, adopt improvements that bring 'the good' into painting and sculpture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several artists (Gaddo, Margaritone) are noted to have departed from pure Greek manner to more expressive, better-handled styles; Vasari treats innovation over slavish tradition as a criterion of advancement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Softness and naturalism in drapery
rubrics_metrics.description: Drapery should be rendered with softness and convincing fold structure contributing to the lifelikeness of figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Giotto's draperies are praised for their softness; realistic handling of clothing is repeatedly mentioned as enhancing overall realism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical cross-training and learning from masters
rubrics_metrics.description: Studying the work of other masters and across media (painting, sculpture, architecture) improves an artist's manner and quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Margaritone improved his sculpture after seeing Arnolfo; Gaddo learned mosaics working with Andrea Tafi; Vasari emphasizes apprenticeship, observation, and cross-discipline learning as routes to refinement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of materials directly affects longevity
rubrics_metrics.description: Materials and mixtures (e.g., gypsum with lime, intonaco constituents) have chemical/physical consequences over time and must be chosen with care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vasari observes that gypsum mixed with lime corrodes and spoils colors, and that negligence in protective measures leads to damage; conservators and artists should consider long-term effects when selecting materials.
